passage: In the school counsellor's small room, with its box of tissues and poster of a mountain, Tenzin and his mother Binita sat side by side for the third time. This week they had brought a sheet of paper. On it, in Tenzin's handwriting: Weekends, home by 9:30. Text when I reach, text when I leave. If plans change, call, don't text. Review in four weeks. Binita had added one line of her own: I will not call more than once unless he misses a check-in. The counsellor read it out. "Four weeks from today, then." Tenzin grinned. "If I'm on time every week, can it be ten o'clock?" Binita smiled too. "Show me first."

qa.q: By what time must Tenzin be home on weekends?
qa.a: He must be home by 9:30 on weekends.

qa.q: What does Tenzin's grin and question about ten o'clock suggest?
qa.a: He feels hopeful and motivated, understanding that being reliable can earn him more freedom.

qa.q: What makes this agreement likely to work?
qa.a: It has a clear curfew, a contact plan, a review date and a limit on Binita's calls, so both sides know the rules and can build trust step by step.

qa.q: What is Binita learning in this arrangement?
qa.a: She is learning to keep a boundary while letting Tenzin practise freedom, trusting him more as he proves reliable.

grounding: It shows a parent and teen agreeing on a curfew, contact plan and review date, with reliability earning more freedom and the parent learning to let him practise.

passage:
Hi Pradeep Mama,
You asked how things are with Papa after all the fights. Honestly? Better. Last Sunday we sat down and made actual rules. I can go out with friends on Fridays, home by ten. I text when I reach and when I leave. If I'm going to be late, I call before, not after. And we'll look at it again after a month.
The funny thing is, Papa also had to agree to stuff. He won't call me ten times, only if I miss a text. Last Friday I was home at 9:50 and he just said, "Good," and went back to his newspaper. 🙂
If I keep this up, he said we can talk about Saturday nights too.
Siddharth

qa.q: How often will Papa call Siddharth now?
qa.a: He won't call ten times; he will only call if Siddharth misses a text.

qa.q: How does Siddharth feel about the new rules?
qa.a: Siddharth feels hopeful and a bit proud, seeing that keeping the rules is already earning trust and maybe more freedom.

qa.q: Why is the one-month review a smart part of the plan?
qa.a: It gives both of them a set time to see how it went, so trust can grow step by step instead of through fights.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when Siddharth came home at 9:50?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved and pleased that the plan was working, which is why he just said "Good."

grounding: It illustrates a teen and parent agreeing on a curfew, a contact plan and a review, so reliability earns freedom while the parent holds a boundary and lets go a little.

passage:
People ask how we stopped fighting about curfew in our house. I'm Ramesh, Zainab's father, and honestly, we made a deal.

Zainab wanted to stay out till ten on weekends with her friends from the theatre group. I wanted her home by eight. We'd fought about it for months.

So one Sunday we sat at the dining table with paper. We agreed: nine thirty on Saturdays. She'd text me when she reached the venue and when she left. If plans changed, she'd call, not text. And we'd review it after four weeks.

The first two weeks, she was back at nine twenty-five, every time. Third week, she called: "The rehearsal's running late, can I come at nine forty-five?" I said yes. That call mattered more than the time.

At the review, we moved it to ten. She earned it. And I learned to let her practise, even when my stomach was in knots.

qa.q: What time did they agree on for Saturdays at first?
qa.a: Nine thirty.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel letting Zainab practise the new freedom?
qa.a: He felt anxious, his stomach in knots, but proud when she proved reliable.

qa.q: Why did the review after four weeks work well?
qa.a: It let Zainab show reliability and earn more freedom, while Ramesh kept a boundary and still let her practise.

qa.q: What did the phone call in the third week show about Zainab?
qa.a: It showed she was taking the agreement seriously, being honest when plans changed rather than just coming home late.

grounding: Ramesh and his daughter Zainab agree on a curfew, a contact plan and a review; her reliability earns more freedom and he learns to hold a boundary while letting her practise.

passage:
I'm Vaibhav, Hrithik's younger brother, and I had a front-row seat to the big curfew fight of last year.

For weeks it was shouting. Hrithik wanted to go to his friends' gaming nights until eleven. Papa said nine, or nothing.

Then one Sunday, they sat on the balcony with a notebook. I pretended to do homework nearby. They wrote down: ten o'clock on Fridays. Hrithik would send a message when he reached and when he left. Papa would not call him every half hour. And they'd check again in a month.

For the first few Fridays, Hrithik was home at 9:55. Once he was late by fifteen minutes, but he'd called at 9:45 to say the auto was delayed. Papa didn't shout.

At the one-month check, Papa said, "You've been reliable. Let's make it ten thirty." Hrithik looked surprised, and then very pleased.

qa.q: What time did they first agree on for Fridays?
qa.a: Ten o'clock.

qa.q: How did Hrithik seem to feel at the one-month check?
qa.a: He seemed surprised and then very pleased, proud that his reliability earned more freedom.

qa.q: Why did this agreement work better than the shouting?
qa.a: It set clear rules on both sides, a curfew, messages and no constant calls, and a review, so trust could grow step by step.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when Hrithik called at 9:45?
qa.a: He was probably relieved and reassured that Hrithik kept him informed, so he didn't need to shout.

grounding: Vaibhav, a younger brother, observes Hrithik and Papa agree on a curfew, a contact plan and a review, with reliability earning more freedom.

passage:
June. After another fight about Yogesh coming home late from football, his mother, Indu, sat him down at the kitchen table in their Jaipur flat. They wrote down a deal: home by seven thirty on weekdays; message when leaving the ground; if he'd be late, call before seven. Review in three weeks.

Late June, two weeks on. Yogesh was home by seven twenty every evening. Once, the match went into extra time, and he called at 6:55. Indu said, "Thanks for calling," and meant it. She was still nervous, watching the clock. But she didn't call him even once.

July, the review. Indu said, "You've been reliable. Eight o'clock from now on." Yogesh grinned. "Really?"

"Really. But the call-before-seven rule stays."

"Deal."

Indu realised that holding one rule firmly had made it easier to loosen the others.

qa.q: By what time did Yogesh call when the match went into extra time?
How did Indu feel during those first weeks?
qa.a: She felt nervous, still watching the clock, but also grateful when Yogesh called.

qa.q: What did Indu learn about holding boundaries?
qa.a: That keeping one firm rule, the call before seven, made it easier to give more freedom elsewhere while Yogesh practised being reliable.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel when the time moved to eight?
qa.a: He was delighted and a little surprised, proud to have earned more freedom.

grounding: Over weeks Indu and Yogesh keep a curfew and contact deal with a review; his reliability earns more freedom while she holds a boundary and lets him practise.

passage: Lavanya, you think Dadi was strict? Let your Mohit Chacha tell you about the summer I turned sixteen. I wanted to go to the late film shows with my cricket friends. First we fought, the usual shouting. Then one evening your Dadi sat me down with a notebook. She said, "Here is my worry: the dark road from the bus stand. What is yours?" I said, "That you'll treat me like a baby forever." So we wrote a deal. Home by ten. A call from the phone booth when leaving. After one month, we look at it again. I kept it every week, even the night the bus broke down; I walked to a booth and called. After the month she said, "Ten-thirty, then." And she was learning too, beta. She stopped waiting at the gate and started waiting inside, with the radio.

qa.q: What time did the deal say Mohit had to be home?
qa.a: Home by ten.

qa.q: How did the young Mohit feel about being treated 'like a baby'?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and eager to be trusted, which is why he named that fear when Dadi asked.

qa.q: What choice did Mohit make the night the bus broke down, and why did it matter?
qa.a: He walked to a booth and called as promised, proving he was reliable, which led Dadi to extend the time to ten-thirty.

qa.q: What was Dadi experiencing as the deal went on?
qa.a: Dadi was learning to loosen her hold, moving from waiting anxiously at the gate to waiting inside with the radio, calmer as trust grew.

grounding: Shows a parent and teen agreeing a curfew, a contact plan and a review, with reliability earning more freedom and the parent learning to let go.
